references.text: They sent spies who pretended to be righteous. The parallel passages in [ref:Matt 22:15-16|Matthew 22:15-16] and [ref:Mark 12:13|Mark 12:13] describe the same plot, where the Pharisees and Herodians were sent to trap Jesus in his words.

Matthew's parallel account describes how the Pharisees plotted to trap Jesus in his words and sent their disciples together with the Herodians—they acted hypocritically and flattered him, as Luke describes with the phrase "pretended to be righteous".
Mark's parallel account mentions that Pharisees and Herodians were sent to trap Jesus in speech, corresponding to the spies in Luke's version.
Earlier in Luke, it is told that the scribes and Pharisees watched Jesus closely to catch him in something he said—the same motive as here in [ref:Luk 20:20|Luke 20:20].

The verb "παρατηρέω" (to watch closely, keep under surveillance) is also used here, where the scribes and Pharisees kept a close watch on Jesus to see if he healed on the Sabbath, in order to find something to accuse him of.
In [ref:1 Sam 22:8|1 Samuel 22:8], Saul uses spies and informants against David—an Old Testament pattern where rulers use underhanded methods to trap those they see as a threat.

The psalmist describes enemies who watch his steps and lie in wait for him—"they gather together, they hide themselves, they mark my steps"—an image that corresponds to the surveillance and spies sent against Jesus.

Isaiah speaks of those who set traps for the one who pleads justice at the gate, and with falsehood bring down the righteous—a prophetic picture that mirrors the attempt to trap Jesus in his own words.
In [ref:Jer 18:18|Jeremiah 18:18], enemies plan to harm the prophet with his own words—"let us strike him with the tongue"—corresponding to the plan to seize hold of Jesus' words.

The purpose of trapping Jesus in his words was to hand him over to the authority of the governor. In [ref:Luk 23:1-2|Luke 23:1-2] we see this realized, as they brought him before Pilate and accused him of forbidding people to pay taxes to Caesar.
The outcome of the attempt is described here: they could not catch hold of anything he said in the hearing of the people, and they were amazed at his answer. The plan from verse 20 failed.

The terms "authority" (ἀρχή) and "power of the rulers" (ἐξουσία), mentioned in [ref:Luk 20:20|Luke 20:20] regarding the governor's position, are linked to Paul's teaching that all authority is established by God—providing a theological framework for the question about paying taxes to Caesar.
